compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.hw_notes: Intel Arc Pro B70 (Xe-HPG/Battlemage class). Wide SIMD, prefers coalesced contiguous fp16 loads. Triton XPU backend likely benefits from vectorized 128-bit loads (8x fp16).
compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.notes: Elementwise add is purely memory-bound; compute intensity ~1 FLOP / 6 bytes. HW fit trivial; focus on saturating DRAM/L2 bandwidth.

memory_bandwidth.notes: Total 16*256*256 = 1,048,576 fp16 elements per tensor = 2 MiB each. Read 4 MiB, write 2 MiB total = 6 MiB traffic. Bound by BW.
memory_bandwidth.risk: Achieving peak BW requires correct block size + vectorization; small tensor may underutilize occupancy.

register_pressure.notes: Trivial - just load, add, store. Block size determines register footprint.

nodes.notes: ANALYSIS: (1) Classification: pure elementwise binary op (add) over dense contiguous fp16 tensors, no reduction, fully independent per-element. (2) Math: out[i]=x[i]+y[i] over N=1,048,576 elements; trivial flatten to 1D. (3) Layout: x,y,out all contiguous fp16 [16,256,256]; can treat as 1D N=1M. Single read of each input, single write. Read-once, no reuse. (4) Regimes: (a) small-N latency-bound: kernel launch overhead dominates; (b) mid-N (this case ~2MiB inputs) bandwidth-bound on DRAM/L2; (c) very-large N pure DRAM BW. Our case is (b). (5) Knobs: BLOCK_SIZE (1k-16k), num_warps, vector width via tl.load of contiguous range, grid shape (1D vs masked tail), mask vs aligned no-mask, num_stages/pipelining. (6) Skeleton: 1D grid, each program loads BLOCK elements of x and y with mask, adds, stores. (7) Families: F1 simple 1D contiguous tiled kernel (best fit); F2 multi-element-per-thread unrolled (loop inside program for fewer launches); F3 grid-stride loop. Primary limiter for all: DRAM BW. Avoid implementation-tactic-named families at L1. OPEN ACTIONS below explore BLOCK_SIZE/num_warps tuning and unrolling vs grid-stride alternatives.

action.description: Implement a straightforward 1D contiguous elementwise add Triton kernel: flatten tensors to N elements, launch grid=ceil(N/BLOCK), each program loads BLOCK elements of x and y with mask, computes x+y, stores. Use BLOCK_SIZE=1024 and num_warps=4 as initial defaults. This is the baseline custom kernel.

action.description: Use a grid-stride loop: launch a fixed-size grid (e.g., based on number of XPU SMs/EUs) and have each program iterate over multiple tiles. Reduces total program count and launch overhead; keeps each tile size modest (e.g., 1024-2048) for good vectorization.
action.rationale: Persistent-style kernel can hide launch overhead and improve cache reuse of address computations; useful if many small programs underutilize XPU scheduler.

kernel_summary: Pure elementwise fp16 add over two contiguous tensors of shape [16,256,256] (N=1,048,576). Fully memory-bandwidth bound on Intel Arc Pro B70; no reductions, no reuse, trivially flattenable to 1D. Key constraints: maximize coalesced contiguous fp16 throughput, minimize launch overhead, choose BLOCK_SIZE/num_warps that saturate XPU DRAM/L2 bandwidth for ~6 MiB total traffic. Correctness within fp16 tolerance is trivial since op is exact add.
open_questions: Optimal BLOCK_SIZE on Intel Arc Pro B70 Triton backend (1024 vs 2048 vs 4096 vs 8192)?
Best num_warps setting for XPU (does Triton XPU honor num_warps similarly to CUDA)?
Does the Triton XPU backend auto-vectorize fp16 contiguous loads to 128-bit, or do we need explicit vector hints?
Is there meaningful launch overhead reduction from persistent/grid-stride kernels on XPU for N~1M?
Are inputs guaranteed contiguous (they are from torch.randn, but should we add a .contiguous() guard)?
Does torch.empty_like on XPU incur sync overhead worth avoiding by reusing buffers?
Will autotuning across BLOCK_SIZE configs add unacceptable warm-up cost in benchmarking?
